title: Schrödinger's cat
subtitle: The most famous thought experiment in physics was actually a critique. Open the box.

steps.title: A box, a cat, an atom
body: In 1935, Erwin Schrödinger proposed a scenario: a cat in a closed box with a radioactive atom. If the atom decays, a mechanism releases poison. Within an hour, there's a 50% chance that happens.
According to quantum mechanics, while nobody measures, the atom is in a superposition of “decayed” and “not decayed”. And the cat, tied to the atom's fate, would be… alive and dead?
Schrödinger didn't think cats could be alive and dead. He wanted to show how absurd it looks to take superposition literally for things our size.
steps.aside: No cats were harmed in the history of physics. The experiment is purely mental.

steps.question: Why did Schrödinger come up with the cat?

options.text: To prove cats can be alive and dead at the same time.
options.why: The opposite: he used the cat precisely because nobody believes that. The absurdity was the argument.

options.text: To criticize the idea that superposition applies just the same to everyday objects.
options.why: Right. The 1935 paper dealt with the measurement problem: where does the quantum world end and the classical one begin? The question is still debated.
It was never done with cats. But versions with larger and larger objects — molecules, tiny crystals — are done for real today.

steps.title: Open the box (many times)
steps.body: Here the atom is a qubit put in superposition (H), and the cat is another qubit that “copies” the atom with a CNOT gate: if the atom decays (1), the cat switches to 1 too. Open the box several times.
steps.after: You only see 00 (no decay, cat alive) or 11 (decayed, cat… well). Never 01 or 10. Atom and cat became entangled: you can no longer describe one without the other.

steps.question: Before opening the box, what's the chance of finding the cat alive (cat = 0), whatever the atom does?
steps.explain: 50%. On its own, the cat looks like an ordinary coin — the weirdness is in the perfect correlation with the atom, not in each one's odds.

steps.title: So why do we never see cats in superposition?
body: A real cat exchanges heat, light and air with its surroundings all the time. Every photon that bounces off it and escapes carries a tiny bit of information about “alive or dead”.

That leaked information entangles the cat with trillions of particles in the environment, and the superposition stops producing observable effects. This is called decoherence, and it's extremely fast for large objects.
It's also the great enemy of quantum computers: that's why qubits are kept isolated, in a vacuum or cooled to hundredths of a degree above absolute zero.

steps.title: How big can we go?
steps.text: In 2019, a group in Vienna sent molecules of about 2,000 atoms (over 25,000 atomic mass units) through an interferometer and saw interference — wave-like behavior, as if they took more than one path at once. There's no known size limit: the challenge is just isolating the object well enough.

steps.title: Physics' other famous cat
steps.text: Schrödinger's isn't physics' only cat. In 2013, physicists proposed the quantum Cheshire cat, inspired by the cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland that vanishes and leaves only its grin: in an interferometer, weak measurements suggest a particle takes one path and its spin takes the other. The effect was observed with neutrons in 2014.
steps.source: Aharonov et al., New Journal of Physics (2013); Denkmayr et al., Nature Communications (2014).

steps.question: What's the main reason we don't see large objects in superposition in everyday life?

options.text: Quantum laws only apply to small things.
options.why: As far as we know, the laws are the same for everything. What changes is how much the object interacts with its surroundings.

options.text: Decoherence: the environment “spreads” the information and the superposition stops interfering.
options.why: Right. The bigger and hotter the object, the faster it becomes entangled with its surroundings and starts behaving classically.
There are proposals (like Roger Penrose's) that gravity might play a role, but this hasn't been observed. Decoherence is well established.

takeaways: The cat was a critique: Schrödinger thought it absurd to apply superposition carelessly to large objects.
Atom and cat become entangled: the results are correlated even though each one, on its own, looks random.
Decoherence explains why the big world looks classical — and why qubits need so much isolation.
